log.question: Walk me through Deutsch-Jozsa for a balanced function on 2 input bits.

route.reason: The learner asks for a walkthrough of the Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm with a balanced function on 2 input bits.

explanation.goal: Decide with one oracle query whether f on 2 input bits is constant or balanced; here f is balanced, using the example f(x1x2) = x1 (outputs 0 for 00, 01 and 1 for 10, 11).

steps.action: Prepare two input qubits in |0> and one ancilla qubit in |1>.
Apply H = (1/sqrt(2))[[1,1],[1,-1]] to all three qubits. Inputs become an equal superposition with amplitude 1/2 each; the ancilla becomes |-> = (|0> - |1>)/sqrt(2).
Apply the oracle U_f|x>|y> = |x>|y XOR f(x)> once. Because the ancilla is |->, this gives phase kickback: each |x> picks up the factor (-1)^f(x). With f = x1, |10> and |11> get a minus sign.
Ignore the ancilla (it stays |-> and is not entangled). Rewrite the input state as a product: (|0> - |1>)/sqrt(2) ⊗ (|0> + |1>)/sqrt(2) = |->|+>.
Apply H⊗H to the two input qubits. H|-> = |1> and H|+> = |0>. In general the amplitude of |00> is (1/4) * sum over x of (-1)^f(x), which is 0 for any balanced f.

explanation.final_result: For the input qubits: P(10) = 1, P(00) = 0, P(01) = 0, P(11) = 0. P(all zeros) = 0, so the function is balanced. Only one oracle query was used; a deterministic classical algorithm needs up to 2^(n-1) + 1 = 3 queries in the worst case for n = 2. (A different balanced f, e.g. f = x1 XOR x2, gives a different non-zero outcome such as 11, but P(00) is always 0.)
explanation.misconception: The speedup is against deterministic classical algorithms; a randomized classical algorithm can tell constant from balanced with high probability using only a few queries, so Deutsch-Jozsa is not proof of an exponential advantage for practical problems.

practice.question: Run the same 2-qubit Deutsch-Jozsa circuit as in the explanation, but with the balanced function f(x1x2) = x2 (so f(00) = 0, f(01) = 1, f(10) = 0, f(11) = 1), where x1 is the left qubit and x2 the right qubit. (a) Write the state of the two input qubits after the oracle (phase kickback) step. (b) Write it as a product of single-qubit states. (c) Give the measurement probabilities P(00), P(01), P(10), P(11) after the final H⊗H, and state what the result tells you about f.
practice.hint: Apply the factor (-1)^f(x) to each basis state, then try to factor the result into a left-qubit state times a right-qubit state, as in step 4 of the explanation.
practice.answer_key: (a) The minus sign goes on the states where x2 = 1: (|00> - |01> + |10> - |11>)/2. (b) This factors as (|0> + |1>)/sqrt(2) ⊗ (|0> - |1>)/sqrt(2) = |+>|->. (c) H|+> = |0> and H|-> = |1>, so the input qubits end in |01>: P(01) = 1, P(00) = 0, P(10) = 0, P(11) = 0. Check: the amplitude of |00> is (1/4)(1 - 1 + 1 - 1) = 0. Since P(00) = 0, f is balanced, which matches the verified result P(00) = 0.0. Only one oracle query was used.

review.changes_made: Changed the function from the explanation's f = x1 to f = x2, and did not use f = x1 XOR x2 because the explanation already gives its outcome. Stated the qubit order (x1 on the left) and listed f's full truth table so the outcome |01> is unambiguous. Checked that the |00> amplitude is 0, consistent with the verified result.
